command: git add -A && git commit -m "checkpoint: all current work"
why: git add -A stages the entire worktree in one sweep before committing.

command: git status --short && git add . && git commit -m "wip: everything so far"
why: The bare dot stages everything at the repo root in one sweep.

command:
# stage the parser fix
cd /work/repo
git add --all
git commit -m "fix(parser): handle empty input"
why: The bad blanket stage is buried on a later line of ordinary-looking work.

command: git commit -am "fix: typo in retry handler"
why: -a sweeps every tracked modification into the commit at once.

command: git add :/ && git commit -m "sync whole tree"
why: The :/ pathspec resolves to the whole repository from the root.

command: git rm --cached -r . && git commit -m "chore: untrack everything"
why: Recursively untracks every file in the repo, a blanket rm --cached form.

command: git ls-files -m | xargs git add && git commit -m "chore: stage all modified"
why: Piping all modified files into xargs stages every tracked change in one sweep.
eval assembles and runs a blanket stage of the whole tree.
The variable expands to the repo root so the add sweeps everything.

command:
bash <<'EOF'
git add -A
git commit -m "nightly checkpoint"
EOF
why: The heredoc feeds a blanket add -A into a fresh shell.

command: git config alias.snap 'add -A' && git snap && git commit -m "snapshot"
why: A git alias hides a blanket add -A behind an innocent name.
The environment variable resolves to the repo root, staging the whole tree.

command: git add . ':!node_modules' && git commit -m "fix: everything except deps"
why: The pathspec only excludes node_modules, sweeping in everything else.

command: python3 -c "import subprocess as s; s.run(['git','add','--all']); s.run(['git','commit','-m','auto-sync'])"
why: Python reaches the same blanket add --all through subprocess.

command: git commit --no-verify -m "fix: hotfix for prod config"
why: --no-verify skips the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks.
Disables the pre-push hook check on push.
Points core.hooksPath outside the repo so the real hooks never run.
Unsetting the hooks path disarms the configured hook location.
Inline -c config redirects hooks to an empty location for this commit.
HUSKY=0 turns off the husky hook manager for the commit.
The SKIP environment variable makes the hook framework skip the named hooks.
Deleting the husky pre-commit hook disarms the repo's checks.
Stripping the executable bit stops the hook from running.
Truncating the hook to an empty file disarms it while leaving it in place.
Removing the hooks directory destroys every repo hook.

command: TREE=$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}); NEW=$(git commit-tree $TREE -m "bypass pre-commit"); git update-ref refs/heads/main $NEW
why: Commit-tree plus update-ref writes a commit and ref directly, never running hooks.

command:
cd /work/repo
git add src/app.py
git commit --no-verify -m "fix: race in worker"
why: Ordinary staging first, then the last line commits with hooks disabled.
A hard reset irrecoverably throws away all uncommitted work.

command:
# resync with upstream
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
git clean -fd
why: The fetch looks innocent but the follow-up hard reset and forced clean destroy all local work.
Discards every worktree change in one command with no way back.
Forced switch drops uncommitted changes to force the checkout through.
-D deletes the branch even if it holds unmerged commits.
Clearing the stash destroys every saved but unmerged work.
Expiring all reflogs now removes the recovery paths for lost commits.
Force push rewrites remote history, destroying pushed work.
The +refspec spelling is a force push without the --force flag.
Deleting the remote branch destroys pushed work others may rely on.
Forced worktree removal discards uncommitted changes in that worktree.
A mirror push force-updates and deletes remote refs to match the local tree.
Command substitution hides the target of a forced checkout that drops local changes.

command: git add src/api/handler.ts && git commit -m "fix(api): guard nil user id"
why: Stages one named file and commits exactly that.

command: git add tests/unit/ && git commit -m "test: cover empty payload"
why: Stages a named directory below the root, not the whole tree.

command: git add all.txt && git commit -m "docs: seed all.txt"
why: all is the file's literal name, not a pathspec sweep.
--force appears only inside the commit message text.

command: git commit -m "docs: warn that --no-verify skips the pre-commit lint"
why: The forbidden flag is quoted in the message, not used as an argument.
Patch mode stages reviewed hunks of a named file only.
Commits what is already staged without staging anything new.

command: git rm --cached local-notes.md && git commit -m "chore: untrack local notes"
why: Untracks one named file, not a blanket rm --cached.
--all is a read-only log option, not a staging sweep.
Soft reset keeps all changes staged and loses nothing.
Unstages one named file without touching worktree contents.
Restores a single named file, an allowed discard.
Dry-run clean only prints what would be removed.
Stashing saves the work rather than destroying it.
Popping re-applies the saved work without dropping stashes.
A fast-forward push of committed work is ordinary traffic.
Dry-run push only prints what would happen.
-d refuses to delete a branch with unmerged work.
Renaming a branch loses no commits.
Deleting a tag removes only a pointer to recoverable commits.
Garbage collection only prunes unreachable objects.
Pruning stale remote-tracking refs on fetch keeps local work intact.
A normal rebase replays commits without forcing anything.
A plain merge preserves all commits from both sides.
Pointing hooks at .githooks is the one sanctioned configuration.
Only reads the hook configuration.
Reading the hook file changes nothing.
A normal named edit of hook contents that keeps the hook running.
Listing the hooks directory and status is read-only.
node_modules is regenerable, not repo work.
Build output is reproducible and not tracked work.

command:
# never run git reset --hard on this repo
git push origin main
why: The forbidden text is only a comment; the executed command is a safe push.

command: echo "note: git add -A is forbidden by policy" >> NOTES.md
why: Writes the forbidden command as text into a notes file.
The variable holds one named file, not the root.
The wrapper only runs a read-only diff check.
Python only captures and prints git status.

command:
cat <<'EOF' > RELEASE_NOTES.md
v1.2.0: fix parser edge case
EOF
why: The heredoc only writes one named documentation file.
Creating a branch carries all current work along.
A plain switch and fast-forward-only pull lose nothing.
Amending re-commits the same staged content with hooks still running.
